title: The Vision of the New Temple Begins: Walls and Gates
summary: Twenty-five years into the exile, Ezekiel is carried in visions to a very high mountain in the land of Israel, where a man with the appearance of bronze and a measuring rod shows him a temple complex. The guide measures the outer wall, the three great gates into the outer court, the three matching gates into the inner court, the tables for preparing sacrifices, the chambers for the priests, and the inner court with its altar, ending at the porch of the temple itself.
story: Chapters 40 to 48 are the last and longest vision of the book, and they answer its darkest scene. In chapters 8 to 11 Ezekiel saw a temple filled with idols and watched the glory of the LORD leave it. Since then Jerusalem and its temple have been destroyed. The restoration promises of chapters 33 to 39 ended with God's sanctuary among his people forever (37:26-28) and the land cleansed of its last enemy. Now the prophet is shown that sanctuary. This chapter begins the tour at the outer edges, moving inward gate by gate; the glory itself will return in chapter 43, and a river of life will flow from the temple in chapter 47.
historical:
The vision is dated to the twenty-fifth year of the exile, the fourteenth after Jerusalem fell, about 573 BC. "The beginning of the year" and "the tenth day of the month" may mean the tenth of the first month in spring, the day on which Passover lambs were chosen (Exodus 12:3), or the tenth of the seventh month in autumn, the Day of Atonement, depending on which calendar is in view. Some scholars also note that twenty-five years is half of the fifty-year cycle of the Jubilee (Leviticus 25), the year of release and return to one's land.

The temple Ezekiel had known was Solomon's, built about four centuries earlier and burned by the Babylonians. No temple would stand in Jerusalem again until the returned exiles rebuilt it, finishing about 516 BC (Ezra 6:15), and that second temple did not follow Ezekiel's plan. The gates described here, with three chambers on each side of a long passage, closely resemble city gates of the Israelite monarchy that archaeologists have uncovered at Megiddo, Hazor, and Gezer. Ezekiel's temple is built with the fortified gates of a royal city.
cultural:
The measuring is done with a rod of six long cubits (verse 5). A common cubit, the length of a forearm, was roughly 45 centimeters (about 18 inches); the long or royal cubit added a handbreadth, giving about 52 centimeters (about 20.5 inches). The rod was therefore a little over 3 meters, or about 10 feet. The plan is strikingly symmetrical, with the dimensions of 25, 50, and 100 cubits repeating, and the whole complex is a perfect square.

In the ancient world temples were often set on mountains, the meeting place of heaven and earth, and Israel's prophets spoke of the mountain of the LORD's house raised above all hills (Isaiah 2:2). The gates and walls separate zones of increasing holiness, an arrangement every priest understood: the outer court for the people, the inner court for the priests and the altar, and the sanctuary beyond. The sons of Zadok (verse 46) were the priestly family descended from Zadok, high priest under David and Solomon (1 Kings 2:35), which Ezekiel treats as the only legitimate line to serve at the altar.
literary: The chapter is a guided tour, a visionary genre in which a heavenly guide leads a prophet and interprets what he sees (compare Zechariah 1 to 6). The movement is always inward and upward: from the outer wall to the east gate, through the outer court to the north and south gates, then up steps into the inner court, and finally to the porch of the temple. The steps increase as the prophet climbs, seven to the outer gates, eight to the inner gates, and ten to the temple porch. The prose is repetitive and technical on purpose, with the refrain "the same measurements as the others", and it slows the reader down. Measurement itself becomes a message: what God measures, he claims and protects (compare Zechariah 2:1-5 and Revelation 11:1).

The outer wall and the east gate
The outer court and its chambers
The north and south outer gates
Chambers for the priests and the inner court

doctrines.note: The walls, gates, courts, and steps create zones of increasing holiness around God's presence. The design teaches that God is approachable only on his terms, through ordered access, not casually.
Fourteen years after the temple's destruction, God shows the exiles a temple more ordered and secure than the one they lost. The vision is a promise that God's presence among his people has a future.
The guide says, "Report to the house of Israel everything you see" (verse 4). The vision is given to be told, so that it can shape the people's hope and conduct.

words.note: Madad, to measure. Sixteen times in this chapter. Measuring marks out what belongs to God and sets its boundaries. The act recurs in later visions of a restored Jerusalem (Zechariah 2) and a measured temple (Revelation 11:1; 21:15).

Sha'ar, gate. Forty-three times in the chapter. The gates are the most elaborate structures described, fortified entrances that both admit worshipers and guard the holy space. The east gate will be the route of the returning glory in chapter 43.
Chatser, court, an enclosed open space. The temple complex has an outer court and an inner court, each a zone of access with its own rules, which the later chapters spell out.
Ammah, cubit. The standard measure of length, roughly a forearm. Ezekiel's rod uses the long cubit, a handbreadth longer than the common one, perhaps the older royal standard.

christ: The New Testament does not describe a rebuilt stone temple as the fulfillment of Ezekiel's vision; it points to Jesus and his people. John says the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and that Jesus spoke of the temple of his body (John 1:14; 2:19-21). Paul calls the church, and each believer's body, the temple of God's Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:16; 6:19; Ephesians 2:19-22). Revelation 21 draws heavily on Ezekiel 40 to 48: John is carried to a great, high mountain, an angel measures the city with a measuring rod, the city is a perfect square, and its gates bear the names of the twelve tribes; but John sees no temple there, because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple (Revelation 21:10-22). Christians who expect a future literal temple read those texts differently, but all agree that the vision's goal, God dwelling among his people, is reached in Christ.

hard.q: Was this temple ever meant to be built, and how should the vision be read?
hard.a: The temple of chapters 40 to 48 has never been built, and readers have understood it in several ways. Some take it as a real plan for the returning exiles that went unused, whether because the returned community lacked the means or because they did not meet the conditions of holiness the vision requires (43:10-11). Dispensational premillennial interpreters read it literally as a temple to be built in a future millennial kingdom, with its sacrifices serving as memorials or as means of ceremonial purity rather than as atonement. Many other Christians, following a long tradition, read it symbolically or typologically: the vision uses the familiar forms of temple and priesthood to picture God's perfect presence with a holy people, fulfilled in Christ, the church, and the new creation of Revelation 21 to 22. Many scholars read it as an idealized visionary program, expressing in architecture what a holy, ordered community centered on God would be. Jewish tradition has generally expected a third temple in the messianic age, and rabbinic sources record that the differences between Ezekiel's laws and the law of Moses troubled early interpreters. These readings differ on how the vision will be fulfilled, not on its center: the God who left a defiled temple will dwell again with his people in holiness.

questions: The prophet is told to look, listen, and pay attention to everything (verse 4). Why might God give a vision this detailed to people who had just lost their temple?
The temple's walls and gates set boundaries around holiness. What boundaries does reverence for God create in your life?
The vision moves inward and upward, step by step, toward God's presence. What does that movement suggest about how people draw near to God?
